back: A disease-causing organism, such as a virus, bacterium, fungus, protoctist or parasitic worm.
A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.
Passing a pathogen straight from person to person, through blood and other body fluids or by contact.
notes: Example: HIV through blood or sexual contact.

back: Passing a pathogen through something else: contaminated surfaces, food, water, animals (vectors) or the air.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, such as the mosquito that carries malaria.

front: Mechanical and chemical barriers to pathogens
back: Mechanical: skin, hairs in the nose. Chemical: mucus (traps pathogens), stomach acid (kills them).

front: How do white blood cells defend the body?
back: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies.

front: Five ways to control the spread of disease
back: Clean water supply, hygienic food preparation, good personal hygiene, waste disposal and sewage treatment.

front: How does a **Blair VIP latrine** reduce disease?
back: Flies are drawn to light at the top of the screened vent pipe and trapped, so fewer flies carry pathogens from faeces to food.
Complete physical, mental (including emotional) and social well-being, not simply the absence of disease.
Infection, genetic defects, chemicals, radiation, malnutrition and degeneration.
Infectious: caused by pathogens that can be passed on (cholera, TB). Non-infectious: cannot be caught (deficiency diseases, genetic diseases, cancer).
